Professional Hems: Choosing, Levelling and Sewing Them

The hem is the first thing a client sees when a garment moves. In this module you learn to choose the right hem for the fabric and style, level it accurately on the body, sew an invisible hand blind hem, and use machine hems that are fast enough for batch orders without looking cheap.

A **hem** is the finished lower edge of a garment, sleeve or trouser leg. The raw edge is folded, covered or bound and then stitched so it cannot fray. A good hem does three jobs at once: it stops fraying, it adds a little weight so the garment hangs well, and it gives a clean line that the eye reads as quality. A poor hem, wavy, uneven or showing stitches where it should not, makes even a beautiful fabric look homemade.

How the curve of the edge changes your choice

A straight hem can take a deep allowance because the folded part is exactly the same length as the garment it lies against. A curved hem cannot. On an A-line or flared skirt, the raw edge is longer than the place it folds up to, so a deep hem forms ripples and little pleats inside. The more curved the edge, the narrower the hem must be.
**Straight trousers and pencil skirts:** about 3 to 5 cm allowance, finished with a blind hem.
**Gently A-line skirts and dresses:** about 2 to 3 cm, and ease the extra fullness with a row of long machine stitches pulled up slightly before you press.
**Full circle or strongly flared skirts:** 1 cm or less, as a narrow double fold, a rolled hem, or a facing.
**Shirts with a curved shirt-tail hem:** a narrow double fold of about 0.6 to 1 cm so it turns smoothly around the curves.
Let bias and circle skirts drop

Fabric cut on the bias (at an angle to the threads) stretches under its own weight. Hang any circle skirt or bias-cut dress on a hanger or dress form for at least 24 hours before you level the hem. If you hem it straight away, the hem will dip unevenly a week later when the client wears it.
Matching the hem to the purpose

Think about how the garment will be used. A lady's office trousers need an invisible hem, because visible stitching looks casual. A child's school shirt needs a strong topstitched hem, because it will be washed often and pulled hard. A chiffon blouse cannot hold the weight of a deep fold, so it needs a rolled hem that is light and fine. Traditional styles also have expectations: a buba sleeve or wrapper edge in ankara is often topstitched, while a lace or aso-oke occasion skirt usually needs a cleaner, hidden or faced finish.

Most hems that look crooked are not badly stitched. They were **badly marked**. Bodies are not symmetrical: one hip may be higher, the tummy or seat may lift the front or back, and shoes change everything. That is why a professional never measures the hem down from the waist. She measures **up from the floor**, with the client standing naturally in the shoes she will wear with the garment.
A straight ruler
A firm ruler held upright from the floor is the simplest tool for marking a level hem.
Marking the hem level from the floor
Ask the client to wear the garment, the correct underwear and the exact shoes. Ask her to stand straight with her weight on both feet, looking ahead, not down.
Agree the finished length at the front first, for example 4 cm below the knee, and measure that distance from the floor with a ruler held upright.
Use the same floor measurement all round. Mark with pins or tailor's chalk every 5 to 8 cm, moving yourself around her, not asking her to turn.
Check the side seams hang straight down. If a side seam swings forward or back, fix the fit first; a hem cannot hide a fitting problem.
Take the garment off, lay it flat and true the pin line into a smooth curve, joining the marks with a ruler or curve.
No client present?

For a trouser hem without the client, measure the length on a pair of her trousers that she likes, along the inside leg seam. Ask her to confirm by voice note or photo which shoes she will wear, because flat sandals and 8 cm heels need very different lengths.
Preparing the allowance

Once the fold line is marked, measure the allowance below it, for example 4 cm for trousers, and trim evenly. Then **finish the raw edge**: overlock it, zigzag it, or cover it with a light bias binding (called a Hong Kong finish when the binding wraps the edge). On thin fabrics you can turn the edge under by 0.5 cm instead. Fold the hem up along the marked line and press the **fold only**, not the top edge, using the tip of the iron. Pin or tack (baste) with long hand stitches about 1 cm below the finished edge.
The hand blind hem stitch

Use a fine hand needle (a size 9 or 10 sharp is common) and a single strand of polyester or cotton thread in a shade that matches the outer fabric, or is one shade darker. Cut about 50 cm of thread: longer pieces tangle. Run the thread through beeswax or a thread conditioner if it knots easily.
Fold the finished edge of the hem back towards you by about 0.5 cm, so you are looking at the inside of the fold and the garment layer just above it.
Hide the knot inside the hem allowance.
Working from right to left (left to right if you are left-handed), pick up **one or two threads only** from the garment layer with the needle tip.
Move along about 0.8 to 1 cm and take a small stitch through the hem allowance only.
Repeat, keeping the thread relaxed. Tight thread will pull dimples on the outside.
Every 10 cm, turn the garment over and check the right side. If you can see stitches, take smaller bites.
Finish with two small back stitches in the allowance and bury the tail.
The blind hem rhythm
Catch 1 to 2 threads
Move 0.8 to 1 cm
Stitch hem allowance
Check right side
Repeat this small loop all the way round and check the right side every 10 cm.
Worked example: hemming office trousers
For example, Bisi in Abuja is shortening new crepe trousers for a client who wears 5 cm block heels to work. The client wants the hem to just touch the top of the shoe at the front.
With the client in her heels, Bisi measures 9 cm from the floor at the front crease and marks with pins. She uses the same 9 cm at the back and both sides.
She checks the old length: the trousers were 7 cm too long, so the new fold line is 7 cm above the old one.
She adds a 4 cm allowance below the new fold line and cuts off the remaining 3 cm, then overlocks the raw edge.
She presses the fold, tacks it, and sews a hand blind hem with stitches 1 cm apart. Each leg has a hem circumference of about 44 cm, so about 44 stitches per leg.
She removes the tacking, then presses with a damp press cloth from the inside.
The trousers are 7 cm shorter, the hems are level in heels and no stitches show from the outside.
Pressing the finished hem

Press from the **wrong side** with a press cloth (a plain cotton cloth or clean handkerchief). Lower the iron, press, lift and move; do not slide the iron along the hem or it will stretch. To avoid a ridge where the top of the allowance sits, slip a strip of brown paper or card between the allowance and the garment while pressing. On dark crepe, wool blends and polyester, too much heat or direct pressing leaves a shine that is difficult to remove, so always test heat on a scrap first.
Iron safety

Keep the iron on its heel when not in use, never leave it on while you step away, and keep the cord out of walkways and away from children. Unplug it at the end of the session. If power surges are common, plug the iron into a surge protector rather than a loose extension.

1. Machine blind hem

Most domestic machines have a **blind hem stitch**: a few straight stitches followed by one sideways bite. With a **blind hem foot**, the straight stitches run on the hem allowance and the bite just catches the fold of the garment.
Finish the raw edge and press the hem up to its full depth.
Fold the garment back on itself so that about 0.5 cm of the finished edge sticks out beyond the fold.
Place the fold against the guide on the blind hem foot.
Test on scrap: the side bite should just catch one or two threads of the fold. Adjust the stitch width or guide until the bite is tiny.
Sew slowly, keeping the fold against the guide. Unfold and press from the wrong side.
2. Narrow rolled hem with a rolled hem foot

A rolled hem foot has a small curl at the front that turns the raw edge over twice as you sew. Start by folding and stitching the first 2 to 3 cm by hand-guiding, then feed the edge into the curl. Hold the fabric slightly to the left and lift it a little, so the right amount of fabric enters the scroll. Trim the edge straight and clean first: frayed threads jam the foot. Practise on three or four scraps before touching the real garment.
3. Twin needle hems for knits

Knits stretch, and a single straight stitch on a knit hem will snap when the garment is pulled on. A **twin needle** (two needles on one shank, often 4 mm apart) sews two parallel lines on top with a zigzag-like bobbin thread underneath that can stretch. Use a stretch twin needle, a little longer stitch (about 3 mm) and, if your fabric tunnels into a ridge between the rows, loosen the upper tension slightly or place a strip of light water-soluble or tear-away stabiliser under the hem.
4. Overlocked and turned hem

For casual knits and many quick wovens, overlock the raw edge with a 3-thread or 4-thread overlocker, fold it up once by 1.5 to 2 cm and topstitch, or use the twin needle. On a coverstitch machine, the overlock step is not needed: the coverstitch looper covers the raw edge inside, giving the hem you see on bought T-shirts.

Worked example: time saved on an aso-ebi order
For example, Halima in Kano has 24 identical A-line skirts in cotton sateen to hem for a wedding group. Each hem is about 180 cm round. By hand, she sews about 30 cm of blind hem in 5 minutes.
Hand hemming time per skirt: 180 cm divided by 30 cm is 6 sections, and 6 sections at 5 minutes each is 30 minutes.
For 24 skirts: 24 times 30 minutes is 720 minutes, which is 12 hours.
With a machine blind hem after pressing, she times one skirt at about 8 minutes including the test and pressing.
For 24 skirts: 24 times 8 minutes is 192 minutes, about 3 hours 12 minutes.
Time saved: 720 minus 192 is 528 minutes, almost 9 hours.
The machine blind hem saves Halima almost 9 working hours on this order, time she can use to finish and press the skirts properly.
Always test on the real fabric

Thread colour, stitch bite and tension behave differently on every fabric. Sew a 20 cm test on a scrap from the same piece, check it from the right side in daylight and wash it once if the order is large. Fixing a setting on a scrap takes minutes; unpicking 24 hems takes a day.

Keep your test pieces. Label each with the fabric, needle, stitch length and tension you used. A small folder of labelled samples becomes your own reference library, so the next time a client brings sateen or jersey you already know the setting that works.

Collars, Cuffs and Waistbands That Sit Crisp and Flat

Collars, cuffs and waistbands sit close to the face, hands and waist, so clients notice every bump. This module teaches the construction skills behind a crisp finish: choosing and fusing interfacing, trimming and grading seams, understitching, and attaching each piece so it lies flat and matches its partner.
Flat collars that roll under: Peter Pan and sailor collars
Choose and fuse interfacing correctly for a flat collar
Trim, grade and notch a curved collar seam so it turns smoothly
Create a slight roll so the under collar never shows from outside
Attach a flat collar with a facing or bias strip so the neckline lies flat

A **flat collar** lies almost flat on the bodice instead of standing up around the neck. The **Peter Pan collar** has rounded ends at the front; the **sailor collar** is square at the back and comes to a V at the front. Both are popular on girls' dresses, school uniforms, blouses and some church and occasion wear. They look simple, but they show every fault: lumpy curves, an under collar peeping out at the edge, and two halves that do not match.
A top with a neat collar
Clients look at the neckline first, so the collar must be smooth, symmetrical and flat.
Interfacing: the hidden layer

**Interfacing** is an extra layer that gives a collar body. Fusible interfacing has glue dots on one side that melt onto the fabric when pressed. Sew-in interfacing is stitched in and suits fabrics that cannot take heat or glue, such as some lace, sequinned fabric and very fine silk. For a flat collar, choose a light to medium interfacing: it should be a little lighter than the fashion fabric, because the collar should bend softly, not stand stiff.
Test-fuse a small square on a scrap first. Look for bubbles, shine, a stiff feel or glue showing on the right side.
Cut the interfacing from the collar pattern, then trim off about 1 to 1.5 cm at the seam allowance edges so the seams are less bulky.
Place the glue side on the wrong side of the **upper collar** (the one that will be seen).
Press, do not slide. Follow the manufacturer's instructions: many fusibles need about 10 to 15 seconds of firm pressure with steam or a damp press cloth in each position.
Let it cool flat before you move it. The glue sets as it cools.
Making the roll: the under collar is a little smaller

A fabric that folds over itself loses a little length on the outside of the fold. Tailors call this the **turn of cloth**. To make sure the seam rolls slightly underneath where nobody can see it, trim about 2 to 3 mm off the outer curved edge of the **under collar** before sewing (more for thick fabrics). When you pin the two layers together, match the edges: the upper collar will bubble slightly, and that extra is exactly what lets the seam roll under.
Sewing, trimming and turning
Pin upper and under collar right sides together and sew the outer edge only, at the seam allowance on your pattern, usually 1 cm for collars.
**Grade** the seam: trim the under collar allowance to about 3 mm and the upper collar allowance to about 6 mm. The layers step down so no hard ridge forms.
**Notch** the outward curves: cut small V-shapes every 1 to 1.5 cm, close to but not through the stitching, so the fabric can fold without bulk.
**Understitch**: press the seam allowances towards the under collar and stitch through the under collar and allowances, 2 to 3 mm from the seam. Stop about 2 cm from each end.
Turn right side out, roll the seam gently between your fingers so it sits just under the edge, and press from the under collar side.

Attaching the collar to the neckline

Tack the two neck edges of the collar together inside the seam allowance so they behave as one layer. Pin the collar to the right side of the bodice neckline, matching centre front, centre back and shoulder seams. On a Peter Pan collar the two halves should meet exactly at centre front, or with the same small gap on each side. Then enclose the neckline with a **facing** or a **bias strip**. A bias strip is quicker for children's wear: sew it over the collar, trim and clip the neck seam every 1 cm, turn the strip to the inside and stitch it down. Understitch facings so they never roll out.

Diagnose common stand collar faults and fix them

Stand collars are everywhere in Nigerian fashion: the **mandarin** or **Nehru** stand on senator wear and kaftans, and the classic **shirt collar** with a separate band underneath on office shirts. A stand collar must stand up evenly, meet neatly at the front and never wrinkle at the back neck. A shirt collar must have two sharp points of exactly the same length.
A necktie under a shirt collar
A shirt collar has to hold its shape around the neck, with or without a tie.
Mandarin stand collar
Interface the outer stand with a firm fusible. A stand needs more support than a flat collar because it must hold itself upright.
Press the neck edge seam allowance of the **inner** stand to the wrong side, for example 1 cm, before you start. This makes the last step easy.
Sew the outer and inner stands right sides together along the top edge and ends. Grade, notch the curves at the front, turn and press.

Sew the outer stand to the garment neckline, right sides together, matching centre back, shoulder points and the ends to the centre front marks. Clip the garment neckline every 1 cm, not through the stitching.
Press the seam up into the stand. Bring the pressed edge of the inner stand down to just cover the seam line.
Either slip-stitch it by hand or **stitch in the ditch** from the right side so it catches the inner stand underneath. Then topstitch the edges if the style needs it.
Do not stretch the neckline

A curved neckline is partly on the bias and stretches easily. Staystitch it (a line of stitches just inside the seam line) as soon as the pieces are cut, and handle it flat. A stretched neckline is the most common reason a stand collar is too short or wrinkles at the back.
Shirt collar with band

A shirt collar has two parts: the **collar** (the fold-down part with points) and the **band** (a narrow stand that attaches to the neckline and carries the top button). You make the collar first, then sandwich it between the two band pieces.
Interface the upper collar and the outer band. Many shirtmakers use a firm shirting interfacing for both.

Sew the collar pieces along the outer edge and ends. At each point, shorten your stitch and take **one or two stitches across the point** instead of pivoting at a sharp angle. This leaves room for the seam allowance inside and gives a sharper point.
Trim the point diagonally, then taper the allowances away from the point. Turn, and push the point out gently with a point turner, never with sharp scissors.
Topstitch the collar edge if required, for example 6 mm from the edge.
Sandwich the collar between the outer and inner band, right sides of the band facing the collar, and sew the band curves and top edge.
Attach the band to the neckline in the same way as a mandarin stand, then topstitch the band all round.

On senator and kaftan styles the stand is often topstitched 2 to 6 mm from the edge in matching or contrast thread. Choose one distance and keep it the same on the collar, the front placket and the cuffs, because uneven topstitching distances are noticed straight away on plain fabrics.

Staystitch necklines and measure them before attaching a collar
One or two stitches across a collar point make it sharper

Sleeve plackets and cuffs that match and close neatly
Sew a continuous bound placket at a sleeve opening
Calculate cuff length from a wrist measurement
Attach a cuff so both cuffs match in width and finish
Place buttons and buttonholes on cuffs in the right direction

A long-sleeved shirt or blouse has an opening at the wrist so the hand can pass through, and a **cuff** that closes the sleeve around the wrist. The opening is finished with a **placket**. Two types are common: the **continuous bound placket**, a single strip that wraps the slit, used on blouses and many dresses; and the **tower placket**, a shaped piece with a point at the top, used on men's and formal shirts. This lesson teaches the continuous bound placket in detail, because it is the one most small workrooms use daily.
A coat with buttoned cuffs
Cuffs are always seen as a pair, so they must match in width, shape and button position.
Continuous bound placket
Mark the slit on the back half of the sleeve hem, usually about 7 to 10 cm long, on the line shown in your pattern.
Staystitch a narrow V around the slit line: about 6 mm apart at the hem, coming to a point at the top. Use a short stitch at the point. Cut the slit to the point, not through the stitches.
Cut a strip on the straight grain, about 3 cm wide and twice the slit length plus 2 cm. Press one long edge under by 6 mm.

Spread the slit open into a straight line and sew the strip to it, right sides together, keeping the staystitching just inside the seam allowance. At the point, only a few threads of seam allowance are caught: go slowly.
Fold the strip over to the inside and stitch the pressed edge just over the first seam line.
Fold the front side of the placket to the inside and stitch a small diagonal at the top so it stays inside. The back side stays extended as an underlap.
Working out the cuff size

A cuff must slide comfortably over the wrist bone and allow a watch, but not hang loose. A practical formula is: **cuff length = wrist measurement + ease + overlap + two seam allowances**. Ease for a fitted shirt cuff is often about 3 to 5 cm. The overlap (where the buttonhole end lies over the button end) is often 2 to 2.5 cm. Cuff height for a standard shirt is often about 5 to 7 cm finished.
Worked example: cuff and sleeve gathering
For example, Esther in Jos is making a blouse for a client with a 16 cm wrist. The sleeve hem measures 32 cm around, and she wants a 6 cm deep finished cuff with 1 cm seam allowances.
Finished cuff length: wrist 16 cm plus ease 4 cm plus overlap 2 cm equals 22 cm.
Cut cuff length: 22 cm plus 1 cm plus 1 cm equals 24 cm.
Cut cuff height: the cuff folds in half, so 6 cm times 2 plus 1 cm plus 1 cm equals 14 cm.
The cuff (without the overlap) closes over 20 cm of sleeve, but the sleeve hem is 32 cm, so 12 cm must be eased or gathered in.
She puts two rows of long gathering stitches on the sleeve hem and puts most of the fullness towards the back of the sleeve, where the elbow bends.
Each cuff is cut 24 cm by 14 cm, both sleeves are gathered from 32 cm to 20 cm, and both cuffs come out identical.
Attaching the cuff
Interface the outer half of the cuff. Press the free long edge of the inner half under by the seam allowance.
Fold the cuff right sides together and sew the two short ends. Trim, clip the corners, turn and press.
Pin the outer cuff to the right side of the sleeve: one end flush with the front placket edge, the other end extended by the overlap on the underlap side. Sew.
Bring the pressed edge of the inner cuff over the seam and edge-stitch or slip-stitch it in place.
Topstitch all round if the style needs it, then add the buttonhole and button.

Gathers evenly spread

Which way do the buttons go?

By custom, women's garments usually close right over left, so the buttonholes are on the right front. On cuffs, the buttonhole goes on the end that laps on top, usually the front edge of the cuff, and the buttonhole runs horizontally along the cuff. Always copy the client's sample or the pattern markings if they differ.

Before you finish, try the cuff closed around your own wrist or the client's. It should allow one or two fingers inside. If it is too tight, it is much easier to move the button now than to remake the cuff later. Some makers sew two buttons a little apart on the underlap so the client can choose a tighter or looser setting, which is a small touch clients appreciate.

Choose the right waist finish for a skirt or trouser style

The waist finish carries the weight of the whole skirt or trousers. It must stay flat, not stretch out, not roll over, and be comfortable for a full day of sitting and moving. There are three main finishes: a **straight interfaced waistband** for fitted styles with a zip, an **elastic waistband** for pull-on styles, and a **faced waistline** where there is no visible band at all.
A pair of jeans with a waistband
A waistband carries the weight of the garment, so it needs firm, stable construction.
1. Straight interfaced waistband

Cut length = **waist measurement + ease + underlap + two seam allowances**. Waistband ease is small, often 1 to 2 cm, because the band should sit snugly. The **underlap** is the extension that sits under the top layer at the zip, usually about 3 to 4 cm, carrying the button or hook. Interface the whole band with a firm fusible, or use a ready-made waistband interfacing with pre-marked fold lines.
Worked example: cutting a skirt waistband
For example, Grace in Benin City is making a pencil skirt for a client with a 76 cm waist. She wants a 3.5 cm finished band with 1.5 cm seam allowances and a 3 cm underlap.
Finished length: 76 cm waist plus 1.5 cm ease plus 3 cm underlap equals 80.5 cm.
Cut length: 80.5 cm plus 1.5 cm plus 1.5 cm equals 83.5 cm.
Cut width: 3.5 cm times 2 (the band folds in half) plus 1.5 cm plus 1.5 cm equals 10 cm.
She checks the skirt waist seam line measures 77.5 cm (76 plus 1.5 ease) after darts are sewn, so it fits the band without stretching.
She interfaces the band, marks centre back and side seams on it, and matches these marks to the skirt.
The band is cut 83.5 cm by 10 cm, fits the skirt exactly and finishes at 3.5 cm high with a 3 cm underlap for the hook.
Sew the interfaced side of the band to the right side of the skirt, matching the marks.
Press the seam up into the band. Press under the free edge of the inside band.
Fold the band right sides together at each end and sew across the ends; trim and turn.
Bring the inside edge just over the seam and stitch in the ditch from the right side, or slip-stitch by hand.
Add a hook and bar or a buttonhole and button on the underlap.
2. Elastic waistband

Elastic waists are common on children's wear, casual skirts and pull-on trousers. Cut the elastic shorter than the waist: a common starting point is about 85 to 90 percent of the waist measurement, but elastics differ in stretch, so **always test** by wrapping it around the body, stretching it over the hips, and checking it is comfortable. Make the channel (casing) about 0.5 to 1 cm wider than the elastic so it can move without twisting.
Overlap the elastic ends by 2 cm and zigzag them in a square or box so they cannot pull apart.
After threading, stitch in the ditch through the casing and elastic at the side seams so the elastic cannot twist inside.
For wide elastic (3 cm and more), a few rows of stitching through the elastic, stretching as you sew, give a ready-to-wear look.
3. Faced waistline

A faced waist has no band. A shaped **facing** follows the curve of the waist on the inside. It is interfaced, sewn to the waist, trimmed, clipped and **understitched**, then tacked to the darts, side seams and zip tape. Understitching is essential: without it the facing rolls out and shows. Some makers stitch a narrow cotton tape or the selvedge of lining along the seam line to stop the waist stretching.

Fitted, dressy garments suit faced or banded waists; relaxed, everyday ones suit elastic.
Comfort test
Ask the client to sit down during the fitting. A waist that feels fine standing can dig in when sitting. One finger should slide inside a fitted band comfortably while seated.

Whatever finish you use, mark centre front, centre back and side seams on both the band and the garment before sewing. Matching marks is what keeps side seams straight under the arms and stops the band twisting towards one side.

Zips, Buttons and Closures That Work Every Time

A closure is a moving part: it is opened and closed hundreds of times. This module covers the invisible zip, lapped, centred, exposed and fly zips, and buttons, buttonholes, hooks and loops, with the measurements and checks that make them both neat and durable.
Installing an invisible zip that truly disappears
Choose the right invisible zip length for an opening
Prepare the zip coil and seam before sewing
Install an invisible zip with an invisible zip foot so the seam meets cleanly
Close the seam below the zip without a bubble or pucker

An **invisible zip** (also called a concealed zip) has its coil on the back of the tape. Once sewn, the garment looks like a normal seam; only the small pull tab shows at the top. It is the standard closure for fitted dresses, skirts and occasion wear, including lace and aso-ebi styles. It is not difficult, but it rewards careful preparation and punishes rushing.
A fitted dress
Fitted dresses and skirts rely on an invisible zip in the centre back or side seam.
Choosing the zip
Buy an invisible zip at least **2 to 3 cm longer** than the opening. The slider and stopper take up space at the bottom, and you cannot sew right to the end of the coil.
Match the zip colour to the fabric. On lace, choose the colour of the base fabric or lining, not the lace motif.
Use a lightweight zip for chiffon, crepe and cotton; a heavier one only for thick fabrics that will strain the closure.
Get an **invisible zip foot** (it has two grooves under it) for your machine. A regular zip foot works only with extra care and gives a less hidden result.
Preparing
Do **not** sew the seam below the zip yet. The zip goes in first.
Finish the seam allowance edges (overlock or zigzag) before inserting the zip.

Fuse a strip of light interfacing, about 2 cm wide, to the wrong side of each seam allowance where the zip will go. This stops the seam stretching and waving, especially on knits, crepe and bias-cut fabric.
Mark the seam line with chalk and mark the end point of the opening on both sides.

Open the zip and press the coil away from the tape from the wrong side, using a low iron (synthetic setting) and no steam. This uncurls the coil so the needle can sew right beside it. Do not let the iron touch the coil directly.
Sewing the zip
With the zip open, place it face down on the right side of the left garment piece, with the coil exactly on the seam line and the top stop just below the waist or neck seam line.
Put the coil in the right-hand groove of the invisible zip foot. Sew from the top down until the foot touches the slider. Backstitch.
Close the zip and check it lies flat. Mark on the second tape where the waist seam and any cross seams must match.
Open the zip. Pin the second tape to the right garment piece, face down, coil on the seam line, matching your marks.
Sew with the coil in the left-hand groove, from top to bottom again. Sewing both sides in the same direction prevents twisting.
Close the zip and check both sides from the right side before you continue.
Invisible zip order of work
Finish and stabilise allowances
Press coil flat
Sew first side top down
Mark and sew second side
Close seam below zip
Doing these steps in this order is what makes the zip vanish into the seam.
Closing the seam below the zip

Switch to a regular zip foot. Close the zip. Pull the zip tape ends out of the way towards the seam allowance. Start sewing the seam about 1 cm above the bottom of the zip stitching and about 2 mm to the left of it, so the two lines of stitching overlap slightly without crossing onto the coil. Sew down the rest of the seam. Then stitch the bottom ends of the zip tape to the seam allowances only, so the zip cannot flap.
Worked example: matching the waist seam across a zip
For example, Tolu in Ilorin is making a fitted dress with a waist seam. The 56 cm centre back opening runs from the neckline to below the waist.
She buys a 60 cm invisible zip, 4 cm longer than the opening.
After sewing the first side, she closes the zip and marks the waist seam and the neckline position on the second tape with chalk.
When pinning the second side, she lines up these marks exactly with the waist seam and neckline on the right back piece.
She checks from the right side: the waist seams meet within 1 mm, so she continues.
The waist seam lines up straight across the back, the zip is hidden, and only the pull tab shows at the neckline.
Common faults

A bubble at the bottom of the zip means the seam below started too far away from the zip stitching. Visible zip tape means the coil was not pressed flat or the foot rode away from the coil. Waving or rippling means the seam allowance was not stabilised. Fix the cause before you resew.
Lace and lined garments

On lace over a lining, treat the lace and its base fabric as one layer: tack them together along the seam allowance before inserting the zip, so the lace cannot shift. Where the lace has a scalloped or motif edge near the zip, make sure the pattern lines up on both sides at the top, because a mismatch at the neckline is very visible. If the dress has a separate lining, the lining is folded back and slip-stitched to the zip tape later, which you will learn in Module 4.

Stabilise the seam allowances and press the coil flat first
Sew both sides from top to bottom and match cross seams
Overlap the seam stitching slightly at the bottom to avoid a bubble

Lapped, centred, exposed and fly-front zips
Choose between lapped, centred, exposed and fly zips for a style
Sew a lapped zip with an even topstitching line
Explain the parts of a trouser fly front
Keep topstitching straight and an even distance from the seam

Not every garment needs an invisible zip. Regular **coil or metal zips**, with teeth on the front of the tape, are stronger and easier to repair. They are used on trousers, jeans, casual skirts, children's wear, bags and jackets. How you set the zip into the seam decides how it looks: hidden under a lap, centred between two folds, deliberately on show, or behind a fly.
Jeans with a fly front
Trousers and jeans use a fly-front zip, a lapped zip with an extra shield behind it.

Sewing a lapped zip
Sew the seam below the opening with normal stitches, then machine-tack (long stitches) the opening closed along the seam line. Press the seam open.
On the **underlap** side, fold the seam allowance so the fold sits about 3 mm out from the seam line. Press.
Place this fold right next to the zip teeth and sew it to the tape with a zip foot, from bottom to top.
Lay the garment right side up. The lap side now covers the teeth because of the original seam line.
Topstitch the lap through all layers, about 1 to 1.5 cm from the fold, across the bottom and up the side. Use a strip of masking tape as a guide.
Remove the tacking stitches. The fold now hides the zip completely.
Centred and exposed zips in brief

For a **centred zip**, tack the opening closed, press it open, and place the zip face down centred on the seam on the wrong side. Hold it with tape or tacking, then topstitch from the right side at the same distance, for example 7 mm, each side and across the bottom. Remove the tacking. For an **exposed zip**, cut a narrow window or fold the seam allowances back so the teeth show, place the zip under the folds and edge-stitch close to each fold. A small rectangle of interfacing at the bottom of the window prevents tearing.
Fly front: the parts
**Fly extension**: a strip cut in one with the front trouser piece, or added, that becomes the lap.
**Fly facing**: the inside layer behind the lap, often interfaced.
**Fly shield**: a separate folded strip on the other side, behind the zip, that protects the body from the teeth and supports the button.
**J-stitch**: the curved line of topstitching on the front that holds the lap, usually about 3 to 4 cm from the centre front.

In practice, the order is: sew the zip to the fly facing on one side, attach the other zip tape to the folded fly shield and the opposite front, then sew the J-stitch from the right side using a paper or card template so the curve is smooth. Finish with a bar tack at the bottom of the curve, where the fly takes the most strain when the wearer sits down.

Needles and metal zips

Never sew over the metal teeth or the stopper of a metal zip. The needle can break and fly up. Walk the machine by hand near the stop, wear glasses if you have them, and keep your face back from the needle area.

Whichever setting you use, test the zip several times before the garment leaves your table: it should run smoothly from top to bottom, the pull tab should lie flat, and no fabric should get caught in the teeth.

Buttons, buttonholes, hooks and loops that last
Calculate buttonhole length and button spacing
Sew a machine buttonhole and open it safely
Sew a button with a thread shank so the closure lies flat
Attach hooks and eyes, hooks and bars, snaps and button loops correctly

Buttons and buttonholes are a small part of the garment but a large part of how clients judge your work. A buttonhole with frayed edges, or a button that falls off after the first wash, is the kind of fault people tell their friends about. The good news is that strong, neat closures come from a few simple rules followed every time.
A square button
Every button needs a correctly sized buttonhole and a thread shank to sit well.
Sizing and spacing
**Buttonhole length = button diameter + button thickness.** For a domed or very thick button, add a little more, then test.
Interface the area under buttonholes, usually the front facing or placket, so the hole does not stretch.
Vertical buttonholes are used on narrow plackets; horizontal ones on waistbands, cuffs and wider fronts because they resist strain better.
A horizontal buttonhole starts about 3 mm **beyond** the centre front line towards the edge, so the button sits exactly on centre front when closed.
Place a button at the point of most strain, such as the bust line on a fitted blouse, and space the others evenly from there.
Worked example: spacing blouse buttons

For example, Joy in Calabar is making a fitted blouse. The first button sits 1.5 cm below the neckline, and the last button must sit 42 cm below the first. She wants 7 buttons. The buttons are 15 mm across and 3 mm thick.
Seven buttons means six spaces between them.
Spacing: 42 cm divided by 6 is 7 cm between button centres.
She checks the bust line: it falls 21 cm below the first button, which is exactly where button 4 lands (3 spaces times 7 cm), so there is no gaping.
Buttonhole length: 15 mm plus 3 mm equals 18 mm. She sews a test buttonhole on scrap with the interfacing and checks the button passes through easily.
Seven buttons spaced 7 cm apart, one sitting on the bust line, with 18 mm buttonholes that open smoothly.
Machine buttonhole and opening it safely
Mark each buttonhole with chalk or a fabric pen: a line for the length and a short cross line at each end.
Use the buttonhole foot and the setting in your manual. Many machines have a one-step foot where you put the button in the back of the foot to set the length.
Always sew a test on a scrap with the same layers and interfacing.
To open, put a pin across each end just inside the bar tack. Cut from the middle towards each end with a seam ripper or small sharp scissors. The pins stop you cutting through the bar.
Dab a tiny amount of fray stopper on the cut edges if the fabric frays easily, testing it on scrap first.
Sewing on a button with a shank

A flat sew-through button needs space between it and the fabric for the buttonhole layer to sit under it. This space is the **thread shank**. Without a shank, the button pulls the fabric, the closure puckers and the threads wear through quickly.
Use double thread, or buttonhole thread for coats and heavy fabrics. Knot and take a small stitch on the right side where the button goes.
Lay a matchstick or toothpick on top of the button between the holes.
Sew through the holes and over the stick 5 or 6 times, in two parallel bars or a cross.
Remove the stick, pull the button up and wrap the thread round the stitches under the button 4 or 5 times to form the shank.
Take the needle to the wrong side and finish with several small stitches through the thread on the back.

Linings make a garment comfortable and hang well; piping, binding and embellishment make it distinctive. A **lining** is a separate inner layer that covers the seams and inside of a garment. It helps the garment slide on, stops scratchy fabrics such as lace, wool blends and sequins touching the skin, makes sheer fabrics opaque, and helps the outer fabric hang without clinging. A badly fitted lining does the opposite: it pulls the outer fabric, peeps out at the hem, or makes the garment hot and uncomfortable.

A common approach is to cut the lining from the same pattern pieces, but to sew the **vertical lining seams slightly smaller**, for example 3 to 5 mm inside the garment seam line at each seam, and to turn darts into soft unpressed tucks. This adds width across the body so the lining never strains.

Attach the waistband or facing through both layers as one.
At the zip, fold under the lining seam allowance so the fold sits 3 to 5 mm away from the zip coil, and slip-stitch it to the zip tape. The slider must not catch the lining.
Hem the skirt and the lining separately. Join them at each side seam with a **French tack**: a thread chain about 2 to 3 cm long that lets the lining move but keeps it in place.

In a jacket, the lining is attached at the hem and the sleeve hems, so it needs spare length for movement. Two folds of spare fabric give this: a **centre back pleat**, often about 2 to 3 cm deep, tacked at the neck and waist, and a **jump pleat** at the hem, where the lining is sewn to the jacket hem allowance and then a fold of about 1 to 1.5 cm is allowed to hang down over the stitching. When the wearer reaches forward, these pleats open instead of the lining pulling on the jacket.

**Piping** is a narrow fabric-covered cord sewn into a seam so it shows as a thin raised line. **Binding** is a strip of fabric that wraps around a raw edge to finish it. Both are made from **bias strips**: fabric cut at 45 degrees to the threads. Cut this way, fabric stretches and bends smoothly around curves such as necklines, armholes and rounded hems, which straight-grain strips cannot do.
A pair of fabric scissors
Accurate bias strips start with accurate cutting at 45 degrees.
Finding the bias and cutting strips
Straighten one cut edge of the fabric along a thread, and find the selvedge (the woven edge).
Fold the straight edge down so it lies along the selvedge. The diagonal fold is the **true bias**.
Press the fold lightly, open it and draw parallel lines at your strip width with a ruler and chalk.
Cut the strips, then join them on the straight grain: place two strip ends right sides together at a right angle, sew diagonally, trim to 6 mm and press open.
How wide to cut

For **piping**, the strip must wrap the cord and leave two seam allowances. Width = cord circumference + two seam allowances. Circumference is about 3.14 times the cord diameter. For **double-fold binding** that finishes 1 cm wide, you need four times the finished width, so about 4 cm. For **French (double-layer) binding**, which is folded in half first and is stronger on lightweight fabric, cut about six times the finished width.
Worked example: piping a cushion and a kaftan neckline
For example, Rahila in Abuja is adding piping in a contrast colour to a kaftan neckline that measures 64 cm. She uses 4 mm piping cord and a 1.5 cm seam allowance.
Cord circumference: 4 mm times 3.14 is about 12.6 mm, round up to 1.3 cm.
Strip width: 1.3 cm plus 1.5 cm plus 1.5 cm equals 4.3 cm; she cuts 4.5 cm for an easy margin.
Strip length: 64 cm neckline plus about 6 cm for joining and overlapping is 70 cm.
From a 50 cm square, the diagonal is 50 times 1.414, about 70.7 cm, so one strip along the diagonal is just enough. She cuts two to be safe.
She cuts 4.5 cm wide bias strips at least 70 cm long, giving even piping all round the neckline with a neat join at the back.

Wrap the bias strip around the cord, wrong sides together, raw edges level.
Sew close to the cord with a zip foot or piping foot, but not tight against it.
Trim the piping seam allowance to match the garment seam allowance.
Pin the piping to the right side of one garment piece, raw edges together, and sew just inside the first line of stitching.
Clip the piping allowance on curves so it lies flat.
Place the second piece on top and sew again, this time slightly closer to the cord, so the first stitching is hidden.

Appliqué, beading, lace and embroidery that stay secure

Decorative details turn a plain garment into an occasion piece. Aso-ebi lace, beaded bodices, embroidered agbada necklines and ankara appliqué are part of Nigerian fashion life. Done well, they justify a higher price. Done badly, with loose threads, puckering or beads falling on the dance floor, they damage your reputation. The difference is in **stabilising, securing and checking**.
A sparkling gem
Beads and stones must be secured so they stay on through dancing, sitting and cleaning.
Appliqué
Fuse a double-sided fusible web to the back of the appliqué fabric, following the maker's instructions. Draw your shape on the paper backing and cut it out.
Peel the paper, position the shape on the garment and press to fuse it.
Place a tear-away or iron-on stabiliser behind the garment under the motif so the stitching does not pucker.
Sew round the edge with a close zigzag (satin stitch), about 2 to 3 mm wide with a very short stitch length, so the raw edge is fully covered.
On curves, stop with the needle down on the outside of the curve, lift the foot, turn slightly and continue. Remove the stabiliser carefully.
Beads and sequins
Use a fine beading needle and a strong thread such as polyester or a dedicated beading thread. Run it through beeswax or thread conditioner to stop tangles.
Hoop the fabric or work over a firm stabiliser so the base fabric does not pucker.
**Backstitch and knot regularly**: secure the thread every 3 or 4 beads with a tiny backstitch, so if one thread breaks only a few beads come off, not a whole line.
Do not carry thread long distances on the back; tie off and start again. Long floats catch on jewellery and snap.
Sew sequins with a small seed bead on top, or overlap them so each stitch is hidden by the next sequin.
Lace motifs and overlays

Lace overlays look most expensive when the pattern flows across seams and the edges follow the motifs. Lay the lace on the garment piece and move it until the main motifs sit symmetrically on centre front, the bust and the hem. Tack it to the base fabric. Where lace meets lace at a seam, you can overlap motifs and cut round them, then join them by hand or with a narrow zigzag so the seam disappears into the pattern. Trim the base fabric away behind if you want a sheer effect.
Embroidery

Whether by hand or machine, embroidery needs the fabric held firmly and supported. Hoop the fabric drum-tight but not stretched out of shape, with a stabiliser behind it suited to the fabric (tear-away for stable wovens, cut-away for knits). Test the design and thread tension on scrap. After stitching, remove hoop marks by steaming from the back on a towel so the stitches are not flattened.

Sections: 60 cm divided by 5 cm is 12 sections.

Embellish garment pieces **flat, before** they are sewn together wherever possible: it is easier to hoop, easier to keep symmetrical, and you can check both sides. Quality control is a system, not a feeling. In this module you build a written inspection routine with measurement tolerances, classify faults by how serious they are, trace each fault to its cause and fix it, and finish with a final press, care card and handover that protect your reputation.

Spec sheet and tolerances

A **spec sheet** lists the key finished measurements of the garment: bust, waist, hip, length, sleeve length and so on. A **tolerance** is how far a measurement may differ and still pass, for example plus or minus 0.5 cm on a cuff or plus or minus 1 cm on a skirt length. You set your own tolerances, tighter for fitted, bespoke garments and a little wider for loose styles. Measure the garment flat and compare.
Worked example: checking a dress against its spec
For example, Amaka in Enugu has finished a fitted dress. Her spec sheet says finished bust 96 cm, waist 80 cm, hip 104 cm and length 110 cm, with a tolerance of plus or minus 1 cm for each.
She measures flat across the bust, 48.5 cm, and doubles it: 97 cm. That is 1 cm over, inside tolerance: pass.
Waist: 40.5 cm doubled is 81 cm, 1 cm over: pass.
Hip: 51.8 cm doubled is 103.6 cm, 0.4 cm under: pass.
Length from the shoulder at the neck point: 108.5 cm. That is 1.5 cm short, outside tolerance: fail.
She checks the hem allowance: 3 cm was turned up. She lets the hem down by 1.5 cm, leaving a 1.5 cm allowance, and rehems with a narrow finish.
Bust, waist and hip pass; the length failed by 0.5 cm beyond tolerance and was corrected before handover.
How serious is each fault?

Garment factories commonly sort faults into three levels. A **critical** fault makes the garment unsafe, for example a broken needle left inside, a sharp metal edge, or a loose small button on a baby's garment that could be swallowed. A **major** fault would make the client unhappy or the garment fail: a seam opening, a zip that sticks, a hem visibly uneven. A **minor** fault is a small workmanship flaw that does not affect use, such as one untrimmed thread inside. Critical faults are never accepted. Major faults must be fixed before handover. Minor faults are fixed whenever possible and recorded.

The more serious the fault, the stronger the action: critical faults stop the garment completely.

Count pins and hand needles before and after each job, use a magnet or pin cushion, and run your hand and a magnet over children's garments before handover. A broken machine needle tip must be found before the garment leaves the workroom.

For aso-ebi and uniform orders of a few dozen pieces, check **every** garment against the checklist and measure every piece at a few key points. Large factories inspect random samples using published sampling tables such as ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 and ISO 2859-1, with an agreed Acceptable Quality Limit (AQL); that is useful to know if you ever supply a retailer, but for a small workroom, 100 percent inspection is realistic and safer.

A simple way to find the root cause is to keep asking "why". Stop when you reach something you can change in your method, your tools or your training. Write the answer down, because the point is to change what you do next time.

Worked example: the five whys on a fault log
For example, Hauwa in Kaduna runs a small workroom with two apprentices. She keeps a fault log for one month of 40 garments and counts the faults found at inspection.
Her log shows: puckered seams 14, untrimmed threads 9, uneven hems 6, loose buttons 3, others 4. Total: 36 faults.
Puckered seams are 14 out of 36, about 39 percent, the biggest single problem.
Why puckered? Most are on one machine. Why that machine? Its needle has not been changed for weeks. Why not? No one is responsible for changing needles.
Root cause: no routine for needle changes. Action: a new needle at the start of every new fabric type, written on a card on the machine, checked by Hauwa each Monday.
The next month, she logs again: puckered seams drop to 4.
One small routine removed most of her biggest fault, and the fault log proved it worked.
Repair, remake a part, or remake the garment?
**Repair** when the fault can be undone without marks: a hem, a button, a short seam section.
**Remake the part** when unpicking will leave visible needle holes or stretching: a collar, a cuff, a waistband. Most of these are small pieces, so recutting costs little fabric.
**Remake the garment** only when the main fabric is damaged or the fit is wrong in a way that alterations cannot fix. Tell the client honestly and agree a new date.
On delicate fabrics such as satin, silk and some crepes, needle holes can stay visible after unpicking. Test on a scrap before deciding to repair.
Honesty with clients

If a fault means you will deliver late, tell the client as soon as you know, explain what you are fixing and give a new time you can keep. Clients forgive a delay that is explained; they rarely forgive a faulty garment delivered on time.
Keep your fault log simple: date, garment, fault, cause, action. Ten minutes at the end of each week to count the faults shows you exactly what to train apprentices on and which tool needs attention.
Machine checks that prevent many faults
Clean lint from under the needle plate and around the bobbin case at the end of each working day, using a small brush. Lint build-up causes skipped stitches and uneven tension.
Oil the machine only where and how often the manual says. Too much oil stains fabric; sew a few lines on scrap after oiling.
Rethread top and bobbin completely when stitches look wrong, with the presser foot raised so the thread sits between the tension discs.
Keep a fabric test strip by each machine and sew a short line before starting any new fabric.

When you train an apprentice, show her the fault log and ask her to inspect one of her own garments with the checklist before you do. People learn quickly when they find their own faults, and they start to prevent them rather than waiting to be corrected.

Hang garments on a hanger that fits the shoulders; fold only knits that could stretch on a hanger.

Each step happens in this order so the garment leaves clean, pressed and documented.
Payment screenshots

Fake transfer screenshots and fake bank alert messages are a known scam. Check your own banking app or bank statement for the credit before handing over the garment. A real customer will understand a one-minute check.
Follow-up and alterations

Send a short message a few days after delivery to ask whether the garment fits and feels right, and ask for a photo if she is happy to share. Agree your alteration policy in advance and write it on the order card or receipt, for example: small adjustments free within a stated number of days, with the garment unwashed and unaltered by anyone else. A clear policy keeps both of you calm if something needs adjusting.

Before the garment leaves, take two or three clear photos of it on a hanger or form in daylight: front, back and one close-up of a finishing detail. These photos are your record that it left in good condition, and, with the client's permission, they become portfolio and WhatsApp status content. Never post a photo of the client herself without asking first.
Keep a small handover stock
Keep a box with hangers, garment bags, tissue paper, blank care cards and small envelopes for spare buttons. When the stock is ready, a careful handover takes only a few extra minutes per garment.

This is the video for module one of Fashion Finishing and Quality Control.
Why this matters
The hem is what a client sees first
Stops the edge fraying
Adds weight so it hangs well
Gives a clean line that reads as quality
A poor hem looks homemade

The hem is the first thing a client sees when a garment moves. A good hem does three jobs: it stops fraying, adds a little weight so the garment hangs well, and gives a clean line the eye reads as quality.
A wavy, uneven hem, or one showing stitches where it should not, makes even beautiful fabric look homemade.
Choosing
The more curved the edge, the narrower
Straight trousers, pencil skirts: 3 to 5 cm
Gently A-line: 2 to 3 cm, ease the fullness
Full circle skirts: 1 cm or less
Curved shirt-tail: 0.6 to 1 cm double fold

Choose a hem by fabric weight, edge shape, formality and quantity. A straight hem can take a deep allowance, because the fold is the same length as the garment it lies against. Straight trousers take about 3 to 5 cm.
On a curved edge, the raw edge is longer than the place it folds up to, so a deep hem ripples. A gentle A-line takes about 2 to 3 cm.
A full circle skirt needs 1 cm or less, as a narrow fold, a rolled hem, or a facing. A curved shirt-tail takes a narrow double fold of about 0.6 to 1 cm.
Worked example
Kemi's three orders, three hems
Formal and straight: a hand blind hem with a 4 cm allowance, edge overlocked first.
Sheer and light: a narrow rolled hem with the rolled hem foot, about 3 mm finished.
Hang it 24 hours, level it, then a narrow double fold, topstitched.
For example, Kemi in Ibadan has three orders in one week. Navy crepe office trousers are formal and straight, so she uses an invisible hand blind hem with a 4 cm allowance.
A chiffon blouse cannot hold the weight of a deep fold, so it gets a narrow rolled hem, about 3 mm.

Her ankara circle skirt is cut partly on the bias, which stretches under its own weight. She hangs it for at least 24 hours before levelling. If she hemmed it at once, it would dip unevenly a week later.
Levelling
Mark the hem up from the floor
Never measure down from the waist. Measure up from the floor.
Client wears the garment and her shoes
Agree the length at the front first
Same floor measurement all round
Check side seams hang straight
Lay flat and true the line

Most crooked hems are not badly stitched. They were badly marked. Bodies are not symmetrical, and shoes change everything. So ask the client to wear the garment and the exact shoes, and stand naturally.
Agree the length at the front, measure it from the floor with an upright ruler, and use that same measurement all round. Pin every 5 to 8 cm, moving yourself around her.
If a side seam swings, fix the fit first. A hem cannot hide a fitting problem. Then lay the garment flat and true the pins into a smooth line.
Invisible from the right side
Catch only 1 or 2 threads of the outer fabric.
Finish the raw edge, press the fold
Fold the edge back about 0.5 cm
Catch 1 or 2 threads of the garment
Move 0.8 to 1 cm, stitch the allowance
Keep thread relaxed; check every 10 cm
Finish the raw edge by overlocking or zigzag. Press the fold only, and tack it.
Use a fine needle and a single strand of matching thread, about 50 cm long. Fold the hem edge back about 0.5 cm, and pick up only one or two threads from the garment layer.
Move along about 0.8 to 1 cm and take a small stitch in the allowance. Keep the thread relaxed, because tight thread pulls dimples. Every 10 cm, turn it over and check the right side.

Press it right, press it safely
Wrong side, press cloth. Lower, press, lift. Do not slide the iron or it stretches.
Slip brown paper under the allowance. Test heat on a scrap first.

Slip a strip of brown paper between the allowance and the garment, so no ridge shows. Dark crepe and polyester shine easily, so test heat on a scrap first.

Why this matters
Clients notice every bump here
Collars sit close to the face
Cuffs are always judged as a pair

Interface, trim, grade, understitch
Collars, cuffs and waistbands sit close to the face, hands and waist, so clients notice every bump.
The crisp finish comes from four skills: interfacing, trimming and grading seams, understitching, and careful matching.
Flat collars
A Peter Pan collar that rolls under
Trim the under collar 2 to 3 mm smaller, so the seam rolls under.
Fuse interfacing to the upper collar
Trim the under collar 2 to 3 mm smaller
Grade: under 3 mm, upper 6 mm
Notch curves every 1 to 1.5 cm
Understitch, roll and press

Choose interfacing a little lighter than the fabric, and test-fuse a scrap first. Press, do not slide, often 10 to 15 seconds in each position. Keep the iron on its heel between presses, and let the collar cool flat.

Fabric loses a little length on the outside of a fold. So trim 2 to 3 mm off the outer edge of the under collar. The upper collar bubbles slightly, and that extra lets the seam roll underneath, where nobody sees it.
After sewing, grade the seam: under collar allowance to about 3 mm, upper to about 6 mm. Notch the curves. Then understitch the allowances to the under collar, turn, roll and press.
Sew every collar on a card template, so both ends match.
Stands and shirt collars
Three habits for stand collars
A curved neckline stretches easily. Staystitch it as soon as it is cut, and handle it flat.
A stand must hold itself upright, so it needs firmer interfacing than a flat collar.
Take one or two stitches across a collar point, trim, then turn with a point turner.
Stand collars must stand up evenly. Staystitch the neckline as soon as it is cut. A stretched neckline is the most common reason a stand wrinkles at the back.
A stand needs firmer interfacing than a flat collar, because it must hold itself upright.
For sharp shirt collar points, take one or two stitches across the point instead of pivoting. Trim, then push the point out with a point turner, never with sharp scissors.

Steam flat, then attach the stand

Waist + ease + underlap + two seam allowances.

Elastic waists and faced waists
Elastic waist
Test the elastic on the body
Casing 0.5 to 1 cm wider
Overlap ends 2 cm, box stitch

Why this matters
A closure is a moving part
Opened and closed hundreds of times
Invisible zips for fitted styles
Regular zips for strength
Buttons that never fall off
A closure is a moving part. It is opened and closed hundreds of times.
This module covers invisible zips for fitted dresses, regular zips where strength matters, and buttons and hooks that last.
Prepare before you sew
Press the coil with a low iron and no steam. Never touch the coil.
Buy it 2 to 3 cm longer than the opening
Leave the seam below unsewn
Finish the seam allowance edges
Fuse a 2 cm strip of light interfacing
Press the coil flat from the wrong side
An invisible zip looks like a normal seam, with only the pull tab showing. Buy it at least 2 to 3 cm longer than the opening. And do not sew the seam below yet. The zip goes in first.
Finish the allowance edges, then fuse a strip of light interfacing, about 2 cm wide, where the zip will go.
Open the zip and press the coil away from the tape from the wrong side, on a low synthetic setting with no steam. Do not let the iron touch the coil.
Step by step
Sewing the invisible zip
Sew both sides from top to bottom, so the zip cannot twist.
First side: coil on the seam line
Sew top down until the foot meets slider
Close it and mark cross seams on tape
Second side: match marks, top down
Close the seam below, overlapping 1 cm
Place the open zip face down on the right side of the left piece, coil exactly on the seam line. Use an invisible zip foot, and sew from the top down until the foot touches the slider.
Close the zip and chalk the waist seam position on the second tape. For example, Tolu in Ilorin matched her waist seams within 1 mm this way. Sew the second side, also from top to bottom.
With a regular zip foot, start the seam below about 1 cm above the end of the zip stitching and about 2 mm to the left, so the lines overlap slightly without touching the coil.
Common mistakes
Three zip faults and their causes
The seam below started too far away from the zip stitching.
The coil was not pressed flat, or the foot rode away from the coil.
The seam allowance was not stabilised with interfacing.
A bubble at the bottom means the seam below started too far away from the zip stitching.
Visible zip tape means the coil was not pressed flat, or the foot rode away from it.
Waving means the allowance was not stabilised. Fix the cause before you resew.
Choosing a zip
Topstitching shows outside
Strong, easy to repair
Casual and heavier fabrics
Needs even topstitching
Fitted and occasion wear
Needs special foot, careful matching
Regular zips, with teeth on the front, are stronger and easier to repair. In a lapped setting, one fold hides the teeth and one row of topstitching shows.
Invisible zips look like an ordinary seam, best for fitted and occasion wear, but are less strong.
Worked example
Ruth's centred zip, safely
Never sew over metal teeth or the zip stop.
Topstitch 7 mm each side of the seam
Masking tape strip as a guide
Cross 1 cm below the zip stop
Stitch length 3 mm, matching thread

For example, Ruth in Kaduna is sewing a centred zip in a navy cotton skirt. She chooses 7 mm on each side of the seam, so both rows fall on the zip tape, clear of the teeth. A 7 mm strip of masking tape guides her.
At the bottom she stitches across 1 cm below the zip stop, with a 3 mm stitch.
Never sew over metal teeth or the stopper. The needle can break and fly up. Walk the machine by hand near the stop, wear glasses if you have them, and keep your face back.
Buttons
Joy spaces seven blouse buttons
Buttonhole length = button diameter + thickness. Then test.
7 buttons = 6 spaces
42 cm / 6 = 7 cm between buttons
Bust line at 21 cm: button 4
15 mm button + 3 mm thick = 18 mm hole
Pins across the ends before cutting
For example, Joy in Calabar wants 7 buttons on a fitted blouse, the last one 42 cm below the first. Seven buttons make six spaces, so 42 divided by 6 is 7 cm apart.
The bust line falls 21 cm down, exactly where button 4 lands, so the blouse will not gape.

Her buttons are 15 mm across and 3 mm thick, so each buttonhole is 18 mm. Interface under the buttonholes and test one on scrap. To open it, put a pin across each end, and cut from the middle outwards.
Sew every button with a shank
Double thread, small stitch to start
Matchstick on top of the button
Sew over it 5 or 6 times
Remove it, wrap thread 4 or 5 times
Finish with small stitches at the back

A flat button needs a thread shank, a little space for the buttonhole layer. Without it, the closure puckers and the threads wear through. Use double thread, and lay a matchstick on top of the button.
Sew over the stick 5 or 6 times. Remove it, pull the button up, and wrap the thread under it 4 or 5 times. Finish with small stitches on the back.
For group orders, wash one sample first, and check the buttons are still tight.
Key points
Remember
Invisible zip 2 to 3 cm longer
Stabilise, press the coil, sew top down
Never sew over metal teeth or stops
Hole = button diameter + thickness

Linings, piping, binding and details that stay secure.
This is the video for module four of Fashion Finishing and Quality Control.
Why this matters
Comfort inside, distinction outside
Linings help a garment hang and slide on
Piping and binding outline and finish
Beads, lace and appliqué add value
Secure work protects your reputation
A lining covers the seams, stops scratchy lace or sequins touching the skin, and helps the garment hang. Piping and binding outline and finish edges.
Beads, lace and appliqué turn a plain garment into an occasion piece. But beads falling on the dance floor damage your reputation. The difference is in stabilising, securing and checking.
Choosing a lining
Match lining to garment and climate
Polyester: affordable, but can feel hot
Viscose or cupro: breathable, drapes well
Cotton voile: light and cool for day wear
Satin or taffeta: bridal and evening
Stretch lining: for stretch dresses
Polyester lining is smooth and affordable, but it can feel hot and sticky in Nigerian heat. Viscose or cupro breathes and drapes like silk, but costs more and can shrink, so pre-wash or steam it.
Cotton voile is cool for children's wear and day dresses. Satin suits bridal and evening wear. And a stretch dress needs a lining that stretches as much as the outer fabric.
Lining a skirt
A lining must never pull
Sew lining side seams 3 to 5 mm smaller, for extra ease.
Sew vertical seams slightly smaller
Hem 2 to 2.5 cm above the skirt hem
Fold 3 to 5 mm away from the zip coil
French tacks 2 to 3 cm long at the hem
Linings stretch less and sit inside, so they need a little extra room. Cut from the same pattern, but sew the vertical lining seams 3 to 5 mm inside the garment seam line.
Mark the lining hem about 2 to 2.5 cm above the skirt hem, so it never peeps out. At the zip, fold the lining 3 to 5 mm away from the coil and slip-stitch it, so the slider never catches it.
Hem both layers separately, and join them at the side seams with a French tack, a thread chain 2 to 3 cm long that lets the lining move.
For example, Patience in Abeokuta saw lace wrinkling over a client's hips. She resewed the lining side seams 4 mm further in, gaining about 1.6 cm round the hips, and the lace lay smooth.
Rahila pipes a kaftan neckline
Piping width = cord circumference + two seam allowances.
Fold the cut edge to the selvedge: true bias
Cord 4 mm x 3.14 = about 1.3 cm round
Neckline 64 + 6 cm = 70 cm long
Clip on curves; final seam closer to cord
Piping and binding are made from bias strips, cut at 45 degrees, so they bend around curves. Fold the straight cut edge down to the selvedge. The diagonal fold is the true bias.
For example, Rahila in Abuja uses 4 mm cord. Its circumference is about 1.3 cm. Add two 1.5 cm seam allowances: 4.3 cm. She cuts 4.5 cm for an easy margin.
The neckline is 64 cm, plus about 6 cm for joining, so 70 cm long. She clips the piping on curves, and sews the final seam a little closer to the cord, so the first stitching is hidden.
Outline a seam, or finish an edge
Double-fold: 4 x finished width
Use piping to outline a seam. It shows as a raised line.

Use binding to finish an edge, such as a neckline. Double-fold binding needs about four times the finished width, so about 4 cm for a 1 cm binding. Stretch it slightly around inward curves, and join strips with a diagonal seam to avoid lumps.
Beads and appliqué
Embellishment that stays on
Press embellished areas only from the back, on a thick towel.
Stabiliser behind every motif
Satin stitch covers appliqué edges
Backstitch every 3 or 4 beads
No long thread floats on the back
Embellish flat, before sewing seams
Put a stabiliser behind appliqué, beading and embroidery so the base fabric does not pucker. Cover appliqué edges with a close satin stitch, about 2 to 3 mm wide.
Secure the thread every 3 or 4 beads with a tiny backstitch, so if a thread breaks, only a few beads fall. Do not carry thread long distances on the back. Long floats catch and snap.
Embellish pieces flat, before the seams are sewn, leaving about 2 cm clear at each seam.
Many beads and sequins cannot take a hot iron. Press them only from the back, on a thick towel with a press cloth, and tell the client how to clean the garment.

Why this matters
Quality control is a system, not a feeling
Same points, same order, every garment
Written down, in good light
Fix the cause, not just the fault
A handover that protects your name

Most makers check their work from memory, quickly, at the end of a long day. That is when faults slip through. Professionals use a written routine: the same points, in the same order, in good light, for every garment.
The written record also protects you if a client later complains. Then you fix the cause of each fault, and finish with a handover that protects your reputation.
The 12-point check
Outside to inside, top to bottom
Hangs straight and symmetrical
Collar, shoulders, sleeves, closures
Pattern matching and seams
Topstitching, hem, embellishment
Inside finish, threads and marks
Measurements within tolerance
Work outside to inside, top to bottom, so you never skip an area. First on the hanger: does it hang straight? Then the collar, shoulders, sleeves, and closures.
Check pattern matching at the seams, the seams themselves, topstitching, the hem, and every bead and motif.
Then inside out: finished edges, a free-hanging lining, trimmed threads and no chalk marks. Last, the measurements.
Worked example
Amaka checks a dress against its spec
A spec sheet lists finished measurements, each with a tolerance.
Tolerance: plus or minus 1 cm
Bust 48.5 x 2 = 97 cm: pass
Waist 81 cm, hip 103.6 cm: pass
Length 108.5 cm, 1.5 cm short: fail
Let hem down 1.5 cm, rehem narrow

A spec sheet lists the key finished measurements, and a tolerance is how far each may differ and still pass. For example, Amaka in Enugu's spec says bust 96, waist 80, hip 104 and length 110 cm, each plus or minus 1 cm.
She measures flat and doubles. The bust is 97 cm, 1 cm over, which passes. Waist and hip also pass.
The length is 108.5 cm, 1.5 cm short. That fails. She had turned up 3 cm, so she lets the hem down 1.5 cm and rehems with a narrow finish, before handover.
Fault levels
Unsafe: a broken needle inside, a sharp edge, a loose small button on baby wear.
The client would be unhappy: a seam opening, a sticking zip, an uneven hem.
A small flaw that does not affect use, like one untrimmed thread inside.
A critical fault makes the garment unsafe: a broken needle left inside, or a loose small button on a baby's garment that could be swallowed. Critical faults are never accepted.
Count pins and needles before and after each job, and run a magnet over children's garments before handover.
A major fault would make the client unhappy, like a seam opening or a sticking zip. Fix it before handover.
A minor fault, like one untrimmed thread inside, is fixed whenever possible and recorded. For small batches, inspect every piece.
Root cause
Hauwa asks why, and fixes the method
Correcting fixes today. Changing the method fixes every garment after.
Fault log: 36 faults in 40 garments
Puckered seams: 14, about 39 percent
Why? Mostly on one machine
Why? Needle not changed, nobody responsible
New routine: puckered seams drop to 4
For example, Hauwa in Kaduna logs every fault for a month: 36 faults in 40 garments. Puckered seams are 14 of them, about 39 percent.
She asks why. Most are on one machine. Why? Its needle has not been changed for weeks. Why? No one is responsible for changing needles.
So she makes a routine: a new needle at the start of every new fabric type, written on a card on the machine. The next month, puckered seams drop to 4.
Keep asking why until you reach a cause you can change.
Care card
The five basic care symbols
Washtub: washing; hand means hand wash
Triangle: bleaching
Square: drying
Iron: one, two or three dots for heat
Circle: professional cleaning
Give every client a care card with the five basic symbols. The washtub is washing, and a hand in it means hand wash. The triangle is bleaching, and the square is drying.
The iron shows heat: one dot is low, three dots high. The circle is for the dry cleaner.
For example, Ijeoma in Asaba's card for a beaded lace blouse says hand wash in cool water, do not bleach, dry flat in the shade, and iron on low, from the inside, never on the beads.
Handover
Press, pack and hand over safely
Confirm payment in your own banking app. Never trust a screenshot.
Test heat; press through a press cloth
Let it cool before packing
Tissue, garment bag, care card
Spare button and spare fabric
Try-on, then confirm payment
Test the iron on a hidden seam allowance, and press through a press cloth on dark, shiny or beaded fabrics. Press, lift and move. Hang it to cool completely before packing.
Put tissue in the sleeves and bodice, use a garment bag, and add the care card and a spare button.
Ask her to try it on, and show her the closures and care card. Fake transfer screenshots are a known scam, so check the credit in your own banking app before you hand over the garment.
